Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We'll walk through the data controls in the Console and the API. Priya's going to demo ephemeral mode and redaction rules, and Liam will cover the KMS bits. Any quick context from Tempest before we start?
[00:14] Dr. Emily: Hi, thanks. We're building clinical note summarization and the main ask is we cannot persist PHI beyond transient analysis. We're also under HIPAA, so we need both technical controls and auditability.
[00:28] Jon: Also encryption keys — we prefer customer-managed keys and proof that deletion requests are honored. We have some internal caching layers too, curious how that interacts.
[00:39] Priya: Great, thanks. Quick show of hands—are folks familiar with Redwood's Console?
[00:44] Kamal: We played with the trial but not deeply.
[00:47] Priya: Ok I'll start at the Console level then.
[00:50] [01:02] Priya: (screen share) This is the Routes page. You can toggle request storage per route — 'Store requests' on/off. Turning it off switches the route into an ephemeral mode where request bodies and full transcripts are not persisted to our long term store. Note: we still keep short-lived in-memory caches for the duration of inference to service streaming and KV cache but we never write those to durable logs when ephemeral is enabled.
[01:25] Jon: Is ephemeral mode absolutely write-zero to disk? We need to prove the data is never written to persistent storage.
[01:31] Liam: Good question. When ephemeral is on, our runtime path avoids the request-logger sink and any batching attachments are zeroed before finalization. There are internal buffers in memory; those are ephemeral and not flushed to our object store. We also can provide a signed attestation and runtime diagram for your security team.
[01:52] Dr. Emily: What about KV cache? Some of our prompts include patient identifiers that might be reused in a session.
[01:58] Priya: KV cache is session-local; if you enable route ephemeral + disable prefix caching, the KV never lands in persistent cache. We recommend pairing ephemeral with 'no-prefix-cache' for PHI workloads. There's also a per-request header you can use to opt-out: X-Redwood-Store: false.
[02:18] Kamal: How about SDKs? We need an easy way for our backend to send a flag per request.
[02:22] Jordan: All SDKs support request metadata — in Node and Python you can set request.store=false in the options; behind the scenes that sets X-Redwood-Store.
[02:31] [02:45] Priya: Next I'm going to demo PII auto-redaction. This is configurable from the Console under 'Data Hygiene' — you can supply regex rules, structured field rules (JSON path), and pre-built PHI templates. I'll run a quick payload to show redaction in action.
[02:58] (demo noise, typing)
[03:05] Priya: Here's a sample clinical note. You can see the right-hand pane shows detected PHI: names, dates, MRNs. The system masks per rule—either redaction with tokens, transform to noise, or token replacement with placeholders.
[03:22] Sara: Can we preview the exact output format in logs? Our downstream ETL expects a certain placeholder pattern.
[03:28] Priya: Yes, patterns are customizable; you can choose \"[REDACTED]\" or \"<PII:NAME>\" or a UUID. We'll include the examples in the pilot doc.
[03:37] Jon: Any false positive risk? We need to avoid masking clinically relevant lab values.
[03:42] Priya: You can scope rules to JSON paths and only redaction specific fields; there's also a review queue where flagged candidates are reviewed before global rule application. For sensitive clinical terms, use field-level allow-lists.
[03:55] [04:15] Dr. Emily: How deterministic is redaction — will it be the same across retries so analytics still work?
[04:20] Priya: We offer deterministic token replacement if you enable 'stable-hash' in the policy. That produces the same replacement for the same input value across requests, which helps analytics without exposing raw values.
[04:32] Jordan: Back to retention — we support retention windows per route (e.g., 0 days for ephemeral, 30/90/365). We also expose a deletion API to purge stored requests for a given customer or route; we keep an audit record of the deletion event itself for compliance.
[04:49] Kamal: Audit records — what do they store? We need to know whether deletion events contain any original payload fields.
[04:55] Liam: Audit events record metadata only: request id, timestamp, actor, action taken. They do not include full payload. If you need hardened separation we can stream audit logs to your SIEM via syslog/CloudWatch or put them into your S3 via signed HSM key.
[05:12] Jon: You mentioned KMS earlier. Can we use our AWS KMS key?
[05:16] Liam: Yes — we support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS or CloudHSM. The model of encryption is envelope encryption; your CMK wraps the data keys. We also support HSM-backed signing for attestation.
[05:28] Dr. Emily: How fast can keys rotate? We have quarterly rotations and need minimal disruption.
[05:33] Liam: Rotation is supported — new keys are used for new writes and we maintain decrypt access for existing objects for a configurable grace period. We can walk you through rotation playbooks.
[05:45] [06:00] Priya: Quick note on caching & batching tradeoffs — with ephemeral and no-prefix-cache, you lose some throughput efficiency. We recommend reserved capacity or Dedicated if you want low-latency and ephemeral guarantees at scale. That's where Redwood Dedicated helps — predictable throughput and stronger isolation.
[06:20] Jon: So is Dedicated required for full PAAS isolation?
[06:25] Jordan: Not strictly — you can get strong controls in hosted with VPC peering and customer-managed keys, but Dedicated gives guaranteed GPU pools and physical isolation. For HIPAA you can run Private in your VPC/on-prem too.
[06:41] Dr. Emily: For audit purposes, can we export request metadata daily for retention reporting?
[06:46] Priya: Yes, you can configure timed exports of metadata and structured audit summaries. Those exports contain only non-PII fields unless you choose to include redaction-safe hashed ids.
[06:58] [07:15] (brief cross-talk)
[07:21] Sara: About the per-request header — if a developer forgets to set store=false, is there an override at the route level?
[07:28] Priya: Route-level settings override request headers in the secure direction: if route is 'ephemeral' it forces store=false. Conversely, a route that stores cannot be forced 'ephemeral' by header. So policy is enforced centrally.
[07:42] Kamal: Great. What about retention for embeddings? We use vector DB for semantic search; some embeddings may encode PHI.
[07:50] Liam: Embeddings can be configured to not be persisted or to be stored only in your VPC. We also have an embeddings redaction mode where we redact certain fields before vectorization. For strict PHI environments we recommend storing embeddings in your own storage and using Redwood private connectors.
[08:10] [08:30] Dr. Emily: Can you show how to wire up the SDK flag in Python briefly?
[08:33] Jordan: Sure. (typing) from redwood import Client; client.request(\"route-id\", payload, store=False) — that sets the header under the hood. We'll provide code snippets.
[08:44] (demo runs, small lag)
[09:02] Priya: I'll run an example with ephemeral on and show logs. (shows console) You can see on the right side the 'Request not stored' badge. If we try to retrieve the request by id, you'll get a 404.
[09:18] Jon: What about backups and disaster recovery? Could ephemeral requests be reconstructed from backups?
[09:24] Liam: No — ephemeral requests are never written to backups. Our backup pipelines only include durably stored buckets and metadata. We can provide architecture diagrams for your auditors.
[09:40] [10:00] Priya: Another feature — live redaction preview API. You can POST a sample payload to /v1/redaction/preview and it returns the redacted output so you can validate rules without processing the request through the model.
[10:18] Sara: That would help a lot for our QA team.
[10:22] Dr. Emily: How do we prove deletion to a regulator? Is there a certificate we can share?
[10:26] Jordan: We produce deletion receipts containing the deletion id, timestamp, actor, scope, and a signed hash. It's possible to provide a signed attestation from our side and you can correlate request ids from your logs.
[10:39] Jon: Are those receipts stored anywhere? Will they themselves contain PHI?
[10:44] Liam: Receipts only have metadata; we avoid payloads. They can be streamed to your S3 or SIEM.
[10:50] [11:05] Dr. Emily: About cost — ephemeral plus no-prefix-cache sounds more expensive because you lose caching gains. What can Redwood Optimize suggest?
[11:11] Priya: Redwood Optimize runs profile runs on sample traffic and suggests quantization, batching windows, and when you can safely enable prefix caching for non-sensitive fields. For sensitive fields we recommend field-level redaction and tagging non-sensitive prefixes for cache. Optimize can produce a cost delta report.
[11:29] Kamal: Are these profiling runs safe with PHI?
[11:32] Priya: We can run them in a redaction-only preview mode where sample traffic is redacted before analysis, or you can run Optimize in your Private deployment.
[11:44] [12:00] (typing, short pause)
[12:06] Jordan: Quick compliance Q: SOC2/ISO — we have SOC2 Type II; I'll share the cert. For ISO or local regs, we can discuss dedicated commitments.
[12:18] Jon: We need the SOC2 and pen test reports to go to procurement.
[12:22] Jordan: Noted — I'll attach those.
[12:27] [12:40] Priya: We'll also include a sample policy JSON for the redaction rules and an example IAM policy for KMS usage.
[12:50] Dr. Emily: Two other items — data residency in EU for EU patients; we have clinics in EU and US. How is routing handled?
[12:59] Liam: You can set geo-routing rules per route — force EU requests to EU region. We also support private deployments for full data residency. And for hosted, you can pin routes to regions.
[13:15] Kamal: If we pin to EU, does KMS need to be in-region?
[13:18] Liam: Best practice is to use a region-scoped KMS key; cross-region keys are supported but increase complexity.
[13:27] [13:45] Sara: Legal will also ask about eDiscovery: if a court requests records, how do we respond?
[13:52] Jordan: We can export matching metadata and, if you have stored request bodies, we can assist with controlled export. For ephemeral mode, there will be nothing to export. We can provide our legal team contact for subpoena handling.
[14:08] [14:30] Dr. Emily: Anything about performance SLOs when ephemeral is used at scale?
[14:34] Priya: There's a small latency overhead because of reduced batching effectiveness; we quantify that in the console per-route metrics. For strict SLOs we suggest Dedicated or increased concurrency in Hosted. We'll include benchmark numbers for similar workloads in the pilot packet.
[14:52] Jon: Could you run a quick stress example to show throughput delta?
[14:56] Priya: Not in this call, but we can run a dedicated perf run and share the spreadsheet.
[15:03] [15:20] (brief conversation about pilot scope)
[15:28] Jordan: Proposed pilot: 6-week pilot, scope two routes (one ephemeral clinical notes pipeline, one non-PHI summarization) — measure cost, latency, and redaction accuracy. If that works we'll plan a small perf run and security review.
[15:45] Dr. Emily: That sounds fine. Procurement will need pricing and the SOC2 docs.
[15:50] Jordan: We'll send pricing tiers including dedicated capacity options and pilot discounts.
[16:00] [16:30] (closing items, recap)
[16:35] Jordan: Recap: Jordan to share SOC2/whitepaper; Priya to send pilot setup + redaction policy examples; Kamal will provide sample payloads; Sara to loop in Legal/Procurement. We will schedule pilot kickoff for week of Aug 25.
[16:50] Dr. Emily: Thanks everyone — appreciate the thoroughness.
[17:00] Jordan: Thanks, we'll follow up by email.

(End of transcript)
